name: Threat Modeling Common Pitfalls
description: This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday threat modeling work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical threat modeling tasks.
content:
This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday threat modeling work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical threat modeling tasks.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Before starting threat modeling work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
2. Surface known limitations of a chosen threat modeling approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
3. Prefer the simplest threat modeling approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
4. Validate threat modeling outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
5. Check that threat modeling terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
6. Keep threat modeling outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
7. Re-check edge cases relevant to threat modeling (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
8. State assumptions about threat modeling explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting threat modeling assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not apply generic threat modeling advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid introducing new threat modeling abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for threat modeling, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
